title_en: Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing v. Di Ping and others — dispute over housing sales contract
ruling_gist_en: A cohabiting family member who, in his or her own name, sells a house owned by another family member to a third party: whether such act is effective against the house owner depends on whether the house owner had prior knowledge and consent. To that end, the people's court shall make a comprehensive determination based on factors including whether the house owner holds the title certificate and keys, the payment of consideration, the duration of the buyer's actual possession of the house, and relevant witness testimony.
keywords_en: civil; house sale contract dispute; second instance; intermediate people's court; Jiangsu Province; natural person; Contract Law; validity of sale by family member on behalf of owner; whether the house owner knew and consented; effect of contractual defects on validity; affirmance of original judgment; house sale; contract signed by family member on behalf; long-term possession and use; good faith; contract dispute; sale contract; Di Ping and others' house sale contract dispute
full_text_en:
Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing v. Di Ping et al. — Dispute over House Sale Contract

Ruling Summary

Where a family member living together sells, in their own name, a house owned by another family member to a third party, whether such act is binding on the owner depends on whether the owner had prior knowledge of and consented to the sale. Accordingly, the people's court shall make a comprehensive determination by taking into account such factors as whether the house ownership certificate and keys are held by the owner, the payment of consideration, the actual duration of the buyer's possession of the house, and relevant witness testimony.

Plaintiffs: Wan Xuequan, male, 67 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Jiangdu District, Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiff: Wan Bing, male, 38 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Jiangdu District, Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendants: Di Ping, male, 92 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Xin District, Zhenjiang City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Guan Yun, female, 67 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Xin District, Zhenjiang City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Ding Qiyuan, male, 71 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Xin District, Zhenjiang City, Jiangsu Province.

The plaintiffs, Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, filed a lawsuit with the Jiangdu District People's Court of Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province, against the defendants, Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan, regarding a dispute over a house sale contract.

The plaintiffs, Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, alleged: On July 5, 2000, the defendants, Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan, sold to the plaintiffs a shell house with an area of 85.12 square meters and an attached garage, located at Unit X, Building X, Criminal Police Brigade, East Dongfanghong Road, Former Jiangdu Town, and signed a house sale agreement. The plaintiffs first paid the defendants RMB 100,000 in accordance with the agreement. The defendants delivered the house keys and the old property ownership certificate to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs then renovated the house and have lived there ever since. When new certificates were issued in 2012, the plaintiffs repeatedly requested the defendants to assist in handling the ownership transfer procedures, but the defendants ignored the requests. Therefore, the plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, requesting that the court order the defendants to assist in handling the house ownership transfer procedures and to pay liquidated damages and economic losses totaling RMB 1,289.20.

The defendant, Di Ping, argued: Defendant Di Ping never signed any house sale agreement with anyone. The disputed house is owned by Di Ping, and no one has the right to dispose of it. The plaintiffs' claims have no factual or legal basis. The court is requested to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

The defendants, Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun, argued: The house sale agreement provided by the plaintiff Wan Bing was signed between the plaintiff and Ding Qiyuan; the defendants Di Ping and Guan Yun did not sign it. Ding Qiyuan indeed received a RMB 10,000 deposit for the house purchase from the plaintiff and issued a receipt. Guan Yun and Ding Qiyuan indeed received a total of RMB 100,000 in purchase price from the plaintiff, and Guan Yun issued a receipt. However, Di Ping had no knowledge of the sale.

The Jiangdu District People's Court of Yangzhou City found the following facts through first-instance trial:

Wan Bing is the son of Wan Xuequan and Xu Bolan (deceased). Guan Yun is the daughter of Di Ping and Sun Xiuzhen (deceased). Ding Qiyuan is the husband of Guan Yun. Ding Haiyan is the daughter of Guan Yun and Ding Qiyuan.

In 1996, the defendant Di Ping obtained a public housing reform unit from the former Jiangdu City Court. In April 1999, the unit began to be demolished and rebuilt. In early 2000, Di Ping obtained the disputed house due to the demolition of that unit. On July 5, 2000, the plaintiffs, Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, signed a house sale agreement with the defendants, agreeing to sell to the plaintiffs the house and garage located at Unit X, Building X, Criminal Police Brigade, East Dongfanghong Road, Former Jiangdu Town, registered under Di Ping's name. The parties agreed on a house price of RMB 108,000. The payment method was: upon the agreement taking effect, the plaintiffs would first pay a deposit of RMB 10,000; when the defendants delivered the old property ownership certificate, the plaintiffs would pay another RMB 90,000; after the defendants assisted in handling the house ownership transfer procedures, the balance of RMB 8,000 would be paid in full. On the same day the agreement was signed, the defendant Ding Qiyuan, on behalf of Di Ping, received a RMB 10,000 deposit for the house purchase from Wan Bing and issued a receipt.

On August 22, 2000, the defendants Guan Yun and Ding Qiyuan, on behalf of the defendant Di Ping, received RMB 90,000 in purchase price from the plaintiff Wan Bing. On the same day, Guan Yun issued a receipt for RMB 100,000 (including the RMB 10,000 received by Ding Qiyuan on July 5, 2000). Ding Qiyuan delivered the old property ownership certificate and keys of the disputed house to the plaintiffs. Since then, the plaintiffs have renovated and moved into the disputed house, and have lived there to the present.

On November 2, 2012, a third party, Ding Haiyan, issued a receipt and borrowed the old property ownership certificate of the disputed house from the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing on the pretext of applying for a new certificate. She later obtained a new property ownership certificate for the defendant Di Ping. As the defendants have not fulfilled their obligation to assist in the transfer, the plaintiffs filed this lawsuit with the court of first instance, requesting: (1) an order that the defendants assist in transferring the disputed house to the plaintiffs' names; (2) an order that the defendants pay liquidated damages and related economic losses of RMB 1,289.20; and (3) that the defendants bear all litigation costs in this case.

During the trial, the defendants Ding Qiyuan, Guan Yun, and Di Ping applied for handwriting identification of Di Ping's signature on the house sale agreement provided by the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing. Because Di Ping consistently refused to appear in court to provide handwriting samples, and because Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun prevented the court from contacting Di Ping directly to ascertain the facts, the court did not grant the defendants' identification application.

It was also found that the wife of defendant Di Ping passed away on the second day of the first lunar month in the year 2000. Xu Bolan, the wife of plaintiff Wan Xuequan, passed away on May 28, 2013, during the proceedings. From before the sale of the disputed house until the time this lawsuit was filed, Di Ping lived together with the defendants Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun.

The Jiangdu District People's Court of Yangzhou City held in the first instance:

A lawfully established contract is protected by law. In 2000, the defendants Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun received RMB 100,000 in purchase price from the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, and delivered the keys and old property ownership certificate of the disputed house to the plaintiffs. After taking possession of the house, the plaintiffs renovated it and have used it to the present. The three defendants have never raised any objection. Regarding the defendants' argument that defendant Di Ping had no knowledge of the sale, witnesses Xia Yuanqing and Zou Fengxiang testified that after the house was sold, Di Ping visited Jiangdu multiple times and discussed the sale, fully aware of the fact and price of the sale. Di Ping had lived together with Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun from before the sale of the disputed house until the present. The defendants' argument is completely contrary to objective facts and common sense, and the court does not accept it. In this case, the plaintiffs paid the price in accordance with the agreement, and the defendants delivered the house. The house sale contract relationship between the parties is legally established, and the house sale agreement is valid. Although the "House Transfer Agreement" signed by both parties has certain defects, these do not affect the validity of the house sale. Therefore, the plaintiffs' request for the defendants to assist in handling the house ownership change procedures is legally sound, and the court supports it. After the conditions for the transfer of the disputed house were met, the defendants refused to fulfill their obligation to assist in the transfer, which violates the principle of good faith, is clearly unreasonable, and they should bear full responsibility for this dispute. The plaintiffs' request for the defendants to bear liquidated damages and economic losses lacks a legal basis, and the court does not support it.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 60 and Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 64 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Jiangdu District People's Court of Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province, rendered judgment on July 9, 2013:

1. The defendants Di Ping and Guan Yun shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, assist the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing in completing the registration procedures for the change of the property ownership certificate and the state-owned land use right certificate for the house (including garage) located at Unit X, Building X, East Dongfanghong Road, Xiannv Town, Jiangdu District, Yangzhou City. The required transfer fees shall be borne by the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing.

2. The other claims of the plaintiffs Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing are dismissed.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 130, preservation fee of RMB 1,920, totaling RMB 2,050, shall be borne by the defendants Di Ping and Guan Yun.

Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan appealed the first-instance judgment to the Intermediate People's Court of Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province, stating: (1) The first-instance trial procedure was erroneous: a. During the first-instance proceedings, the appellants had separately filed another lawsuit with the court of first instance, but the court of first instance did not suspend the trial of this case, violating statutory procedures; b. The court of first instance's failure to grant the appellants' application for handwriting identification violated statutory procedures; c. A piece of evidence provided by the appellants during the first-instance trial and cross-examined by the appellees in court, namely the "Certificate" issued by the Working Committee of Dagang Street, Zhenjiang New District, was not reflected in the first-instance judgment. (2) The first-instance findings of fact were erroneous: a. The house sale agreement in dispute in this case has defects, mainly manifested in the different parties to the sale. In the agreement provided by the appellees Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, the sellers were Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan, and the buyers were Wan Xuequan, Wan Bing, and Xu Bolan. In the agreement provided by the appellants, the seller was only Wan Bing. This defect is a matter of contract subject matter and is sufficient to affect the validity of the contract. If the agreement provided by the appellees is forged, then Wan Xuequan and Xu Bolan should not be parties to this case, Ding Qiyuan's disposal would be unauthorized, and Di Ping would not be obligated under the contract. b. The "Certificate" issued by the Working Committee of Dagang Street, Zhenjiang New District, provided by the appellants, proves that Di Ping could not have gone to Jiangdu alone, demonstrating that the testimony of the witnesses provided by the appellees is false and should not be admitted.

The appellees Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing jointly argued: The court of first instance made clear findings of fact with sufficient evidence, and the first-instance judgment had lawful procedures and correct application of law. They requested that the appeal be dismissed.

The Intermediate People's Court of Yangzhou City, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

Additionally, it was found that the appellant Ding Qiyuan and the appellees Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing each provided a copy of the house transfer agreement. The differences between the two agreements were: in the agreement provided by Ding Qiyuan, the seller's signature at the heading and end was only Ding Qiyuan, and the buyer's signature was only Wan Bing; in the agreement provided by Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, the seller's signature at the heading was Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun, and at the end was Ding Qiyuan, Di Ping, and Guan Yun, while the buyer's signature at the heading was Wan Bing, and at the end was Wan Xuequan, Wan Bing, and Xu Bolan. In the agreement provided by Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing, an additional supplementary clause was added below the signatures: "3. If Party B handles notarization, Party A is responsible for handling the required written documents for Party A, and Party B is responsible for the notarization fees. Party A agrees, please sign: Guan Yun." Otherwise, the contents of the two agreements were identical.

During the first-instance trial, the three appellants submitted to the court of first instance a "Certificate" issued by the Working Committee of Dagang Street, Zhenjiang New District, which mainly stated that Di Ping has poor hearing and could only participate in Party organizational activities when accompanied by his children.

During the trial of this case, the separate lawsuit filed by the appellants Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan seeking to invalidate the "House Transfer Agreement" provided by the appellees was dismissed by the court of first instance and the court of second instance on the ground of *res judicata*.

The Intermediate People's Court of Yangzhou City held in the second-instance trial:

The issues in dispute in this second-instance trial were: whether the house sale transaction in dispute was valid; and whether the court of first instance's application of procedure was improper.

I. Regarding the validity of the house sale transaction in dispute

(1) The disputed house in this case should be jointly owned by the appellants Di Ping and Guan Yun. The disputed house was legitimate property acquired by Di Ping and the third party Sun Xiuzhen during their marriage, and should be jointly owned by the spouses. Sun Xiuzhen passed away on the second day of the first lunar month in 2000. The share of the disputed house attributable to Sun Xiuzhen should be inherited as part of the estate by her spouse Di Ping and her daughter Guan Yun in accordance with the law. Before Guan Yun either expressly relinquishes her inheritance or the property is partitioned, the disputed house should be jointly owned by Di Ping and Guan Yun.

(2) The house sale agreement in this case is binding on both appellants Di Ping and Guan Yun.

First, appellant Ding Qiyuan has no objection to the fact that he reached a transfer agreement with appellee Wan Bing for the disputed house, and to the main terms and conditions of the agreement. Accordingly, it can be determined that Ding Qiyuan, as the seller, signed a transfer agreement with Wan Bing for the disputed house.

Second, appellant Guan Yun has no objection to the receipt for RMB 100,000 as the purchase price for the house issued on August 22, 2000. Therefore, it should be determined that Guan Yun, as a co-owner of the house, knew of and consented to the transfer of the house by her spouse Ding Qiyuan.

Third, appellant Di Ping lived together with appellants Ding Qiyuan and Guan Yun from before the sale of the disputed house until the time this lawsuit was filed. It should be determined that the three were family members living together. Di Ping gave the keys and property ownership certificate of the disputed house to Ding Qiyuan for safekeeping, and these were in fact delivered to the appellees Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing. Moreover, during the approximately 12 years from the time of the house sale until the filing of this lawsuit, Di Ping never raised any objection to the sale of the disputed house or the payment of the purchase price. This fully demonstrates that he had prior knowledge of and consented to the sale of the disputed house. Witnesses Xia Yuanqing and Zou Fengxiang, who live adjacent to the disputed house, testified in court that after the sale of the house, Di Ping visited the disputed house where Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing were living, further corroborating that Di Ping knew of the house sale. The "Certificate" issued by the Working Committee of Dagang Street, Zhenjiang New District, provided by the three appellants, was intended to prove that Di Ping could not have gone to Jiangdu alone. The court considers that this "Certificate" is an explanation of Di Ping's participation in Party organizational activities, and from its content, it also cannot exclude the possibility that Di Ping had returned from Zhenjiang to Jiangdu. The probative force of this "Certificate" is clearly weaker than the witness testimony. The content of the witness testimony has probative value and should be admitted. Di Ping's above conduct is sufficient to prove that he knew of and consented to the transfer of the disputed house. His appellate argument that he had no knowledge of the house sale does not conform to common sense and reason, and is not supported.

Fourth, appellee Wan Xuequan should be a proper party to this case. Appellee Wan Bing and Wan Xuequan are father and son. During the trial, Wan Bing stated that the purchase money was family property. The old property ownership certificate of the disputed house, taken away by the third party Ding Haiyan, was also from Wan Xuequan. Furthermore, Wan Xuequan has always lived in the disputed house. Therefore, Wan Xuequan should be considered a joint buyer of the disputed house and a proper party to this case.

In conclusion, appellant Ding Qiyuan, as a family member living together and with the knowledge and consent of appellants Di Ping and Guan Yun, transferred the disputed house to appellees Wan Xuequan and Wan Bing. This house transfer agreement is directly binding on Di Ping and Guan Yun. The house sale transaction in dispute is valid. The appellant's argument that Ding Qiyuan's disposition was unauthorized has no factual basis and is not supported.

II. Regarding whether the trial procedure of the court of first instance was improper

The court considers that the trial procedure of the first instance complied with legal provisions and was not improper. (1) The court of first instance's failure to rule to suspend the case was in accordance with the law. Whether the house sale agreement in question is valid is a matter that needs to be examined in this case. The separate lawsuit filed by the appellants Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan during the first-instance proceedings does not fall within the circumstances requiring suspension of trial as provided in Article 150(5) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, the appellants' ground of appeal that the court of first instance should have suspended the trial of this case cannot be sustained.

The court of first instance's refusal to grant the application for identification filed by the appellants Di Ping, Guan Yun, and Ding Qiyuan was in accordance with the law. Article 76 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides that "a party may apply to the people's court for appraisal of specialized issues for the purpose of ascertaining the facts." According to this provision, the scope of a party's application for appraisal must relate to specialized issues and must be necessary for ascertaining the facts of the case. From the above analysis, Ding Qiyuan, as a family member living together, sold the house with the consent of the property owners, and this act is binding on the property owners. Whether the property owners Di Ping and Guan Yun signed the transfer agreement does not affect the validity of the transfer of the disputed house. Therefore, the appellant's application for handwriting identification of the seller's signature on the transfer agreement is irrelevant to ascertaining the facts of this case. The court of first instance's refusal to grant the identification application has a legal basis.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 170(1)(i) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Intermediate People's Court of Yangzhou City, Jiangsu Province, rendered judgment on March 20, 2014:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
